title: Exploitation for Stealth
summary: Exploitation for stealth covers the use of a software flaw not to gain more access but to keep existing access hidden. An adversary abuses a bug in a logging pipeline, a monitoring agent, a security product or a cloud control plane so that activity stops producing records, alerts are dropped, or work happens inside a component that telemetry does not cover. The aim is to avoid tripping defences without switching them off, because disabling a control is itself a loud event. Useful signals include gaps in an expected log stream, agents that stop reporting while still running, unexpected version or configuration changes on logging components, and control plane calls that alter audit settings. The distinction from legitimate operations is process: changing logging configuration is normally a change managed action by an identifiable administrator from a known management host, not a side effect of an exploit against a service or an interface.

beginner.definition: This technique means using a software mistake to hide what you are doing. The attacker does not switch off the alarm, because that would be noticed. Instead they make the alarm stop recording the facts. They then stay in the network quietly for as long as they can.
beginner.whyItMatters: Being seen is the biggest risk for an attacker inside a network. If they can silence the records, they can work slowly and carefully. Your team then has no evidence to follow. Gaps in logs are easy to miss unless somebody checks for them. This is why checking that logs still arrive matters as much as searching them.
howItWorks: The attacker studies the defences in place, often after gaining an initial foothold.
They look for a flaw in a logging tool, a security agent or a cloud service.
They trigger the flaw so that records are dropped, changed or never created.
Alerts that depend on those records never fire, while the tool still looks healthy.
The attacker then works inside the gap, keeping access and copying data.
They may repeat the trick on other sensors so no single source shows the whole picture.
beginner.example: Think of a shop with a camera system. A thief could smash the cameras, but the crash would bring security at once. Instead they notice that the recorder drops the last few minutes of every hour when its storage is nearly full. So they fill the storage quietly, then work during the blind moments. The cameras still show a green light and the guard sees nothing unusual on the screen.
takeaways: Hiding is often better for an attacker than switching a defence off completely.
Check that logs are still arriving and complete, not only that you own the tool.
A silent sensor that is still running is a strong warning sign worth chasing.

objectives: Explain why an adversary might exploit a flaw purely to avoid detection.
Describe how logging pipelines and security agents can be abused to drop records.
Identify the signs of a telemetry gap, such as an agent that stops reporting.
Compare legitimate logging configuration changes with exploit driven tampering.
Describe how to validate that audit settings still cover the activity you expect.
